result: EPAC1 and EPAC2 are localized to parallel fiber (PF) terminals in cerebellar synaptosomes, as demonstrated by their colocalization with vGluT1, which is enriched at PF terminals. PF synapses constitute the majority (88.8%) of cerebellar synaptosomes.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1B) showing EPAC1/EPAC2 overlap with vGluT1, and quantitative data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing PF synapses constitute 88.8% of synaptosomes. The localization is further validated by citation to prior work establishing vGluT1 as a PF marker.

result: EPAC1 and EPAC2 interact with RIM1 and specifically induce threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α without affecting serine phosphorylation. Treatment with 8-pCPT (EPAC activator) increases RIM1 p-Thr but not p-Ser in synaptosomes and HEK cells.
evaluation: Claims C5-C11 are supported by co-IP data (Figure 1C) showing EPAC-RIM1 interaction, and western blot data (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) demonstrating selective threonine phosphorylation. The specificity for threonine over serine phosphorylation is consistently shown across multiple experimental systems.

result: cAMP induces EPAC-dependent threonine phosphorylation of RIM1. Forskolin increases RIM1 p-Thr, which is blocked by EPAC inhibitor ESI-09. Genetic deletion of EPAC (Rapgef3/4-dKO) significantly reduces RIM1 p-Thr without affecting p-Ser or total RIM1 expression.
evaluation: Claims C12-C21 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 1E) showing forskolin-induced RIM1 p-Thr is blocked by ESI-09, and genetic experiments (Figure 1F) showing reduced RIM1 p-Thr in EPAC knockout mice. The data consistently demonstrate EPAC is necessary and sufficient for RIM1 threonine phosphorylation.

result: EPAC deficiency does not affect cerebellar structure, as lobule thickness and Purkinje cell spine density are unchanged in Rapgef3/4-dKO mice.
evaluation: Claims C19-C20 are supported by Nissl and Golgi staining data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B) showing no differences in lobule thickness or spine density between WT and EPAC knockout mice. This establishes that the molecular changes occur without gross structural alterations.

result: The authors hypothesize that EPAC acts on RIM1 through the Rap1-PLCε-PKCε signaling module, based on prior studies showing this pathway is activated by EPAC in other cell types.
evaluation: Claim C23 is explicitly stated as a hypothesis. While claims C24-C26 cite prior work showing EPAC activates this pathway in other cell types, these citations do not directly demonstrate this mechanism operates at cerebellar synapses. The hypothesis requires experimental validation in the current system.

result: EPAC activates PKCε specifically at parallel fiber synapses. EPAC expression increases PKCε-S729 phosphorylation but not PKCα phosphorylation in HEK cells. PKCε colocalizes with vGluT1 in synaptosomes, and 8-pCPT treatment increases PKCε-S729 phosphorylation. EPAC deletion reduces PKCε-S729 phosphorylation without affecting PKCα.
evaluation: Claims C27-C35 are supported by western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, Figure 1I-J) showing EPAC selectively regulates PKCε but not PKCα phosphorylation, and immunostaining data (Figure 1H) showing PKCε localization at PF synapses. The specificity for PKCε over PKCα is consistently demonstrated.

result: PKCε binds to RIM1α and regulates its threonine phosphorylation. PKCε expression increases RIM1α p-Thr in HEK cells, and PKCε deletion (Prkce-cKO) reduces RIM1 p-Thr in synaptosomes without affecting p-Ser or total RIM1 levels.
evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by co-IP data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B) showing PKCε-RIM1α interaction, and western blot data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C, Figure 1K) demonstrating PKCε regulates RIM1 threonine phosphorylation. The data establish PKCε as a regulator of RIM1 phosphorylation.

result: EPAC-induced RIM1 threonine phosphorylation requires PKCε. The PKCε inhibitor εV1-2 blocks 8-pCPT-induced RIM1 p-Thr, while PKCα/β inhibitor Gö6976 has no effect. In Prkce-cKO synaptosomes, 8-pCPT fails to increase RIM1 phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C42-C50 are supported by pharmacological experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D-E) showing selective blockade by PKCε inhibitor but not PKCα/β inhibitor, and genetic experiments (Figure 1L) showing 8-pCPT has no effect in PKCε knockout synaptosomes. The data establish PKCε as the required kinase downstream of EPAC.

result: EPAC and PKCε regulate docking of presynaptic vesicles at PF-PC synapses. Deletion of EPAC or PKCε significantly reduces the number of docked vesicles without affecting postsynaptic density, synaptic cleft size, or total vesicle number in terminals.
evaluation: Claims C53-C61 are supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 2A-B) showing reduced docked vesicles in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice, with specific quantification demonstrating the effect is limited to the docked pool. The structural specificity strengthens the conclusion that EPAC-PKCε regulates vesicle docking.

result: EPAC and PKCε are important for presynaptic transmitter release at PF-PC synapses. Deletion of EPAC or PKCε reduces mEPSC frequency without affecting amplitude, decreases release probability (Pr), and reduces evoked EPSCs across all stimulation intensities.
evaluation: Claims C62-C70 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 2C-F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing consistent presynaptic deficits in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice. The selective reduction in frequency without amplitude changes, combined with reduced Pr, provides strong evidence for a presynaptic release deficit.

result: Deficiency of EPAC or PKCε impairs protein interactions in the Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 tripartite complex. Both Munc13-1 and Rab3A show significantly weaker binding to RIM1α in EPAC and PKCε knockout synaptosomes, without changes in total protein expression.
evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by co-IP data (Figure 2G-H) showing reduced binding of Munc13-1 and Rab3A to RIM1α in knockout mice, with western blots confirming unchanged total protein levels. The data demonstrate that EPAC-PKCε regulates complex assembly rather than protein expression.

result: EPAC and PKCε are sufficient to promote formation of the Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 tripartite complex. Treatment with 8-pCPT or PKCε activator FR236924 increases binding of Munc13-1 and Rab3A to RIM1, effects that are blocked by PKCε inhibition or deletion.
evaluation: Claims C76-C82 are supported by co-IP data (Figure 2I-K) showing pharmacological activation of EPAC or PKCε increases complex formation, with appropriate controls demonstrating PKCε dependence. The bidirectional manipulation (loss and gain of function) strongly supports the conclusion.

result: Presynaptic EPAC is required for presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses. Tetanus stimulation (8 Hz, 5 min) induces LTP with decreased PPF in control mice, but fails to induce LTP in mice with global or granule cell-specific EPAC deletion.
evaluation: Claims C84-C91 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 3B-G) showing LTP induction in controls but not EPAC knockout mice. The use of both global and cell-specific knockouts, combined with PPF measurements indicating presynaptic mechanisms, provides strong evidence for presynaptic EPAC requirement.

result: Presynaptic PKCε is required for presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of PKCε completely blocks the induction of presynaptic LTP.
evaluation: Claims C92-C95 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 3H-K, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F) showing LTP blockade in PKCε knockout mice and with εV1-2 inhibitor. The convergence of genetic and pharmacological approaches strengthens the conclusion.

result: The requirement for EPAC and PKCε in presynaptic LTP is independent of experimental conditions. Presynaptic LTP is blocked in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice across different ages (P21 and 2 months), temperatures (room temperature and 32°C), and calcium concentrations (2 mM and 0.5 mM).
evaluation: Claims C96-C109 are supported by extensive electrophysiology data (Figure 3—figure supplements 2-4) showing consistent LTP blockade across multiple experimental conditions. The robustness across conditions strengthens the conclusion that EPAC-PKCε is a core requirement for presynaptic LTP.

result: Presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses occurs upon a rise in cellular cAMP levels. Preincubation with forskolin (which increases cAMP) prevents further LTP induction by tetanus stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B) showing forskolin pretreatment occludes LTP. This occlusion experiment provides evidence that cAMP elevation is involved in LTP induction, though the interpretation assumes forskolin saturates the relevant pathway.

result: EPAC, PKCε, and PKA all mediate cAMP-induced potentiation of transmitter release, with EPAC-PKCε playing the most prominent role. Forskolin induces large EPSC potentiation in controls, which is reduced by EPAC or PKCε deletion and further reduced by PKA inhibition. Combined blockade of EPAC and PKA completely eliminates forskolin's effect.
evaluation: Claims C114-C120 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing graded reductions in forskolin-induced potentiation with EPAC/PKCε deletion and PKA inhibition. The quantitative comparison demonstrates EPAC-PKCε has a larger effect than PKA, supporting the conclusion about relative contributions.

result: EPAC and PKCε function synergistically on synaptic release at PF-PC synapses. Forskolin reduces PPF ratio in controls, but this reduction is significantly attenuated when EPAC, PKCε, and PKA are all blocked.
evaluation: Claims C121-C123 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 4C) showing PPF changes parallel the EPSC amplitude changes. The PPF data provide additional evidence for presynaptic mechanisms and support the synergistic function interpretation.

result: Direct EPAC activation with 8-pCPT is sufficient to potentiate PF-EPSCs and reduce PPF, effects that require PKCε. The 8-pCPT-induced potentiation is abolished in PKCε knockout mice or by PKCε inhibitor εV1-2.
evaluation: Claims C124-C129 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 4D-F) showing 8-pCPT effects are blocked by PKCε deletion or inhibition. The data establish EPAC-PKCε as the dominant pathway for cAMP-induced potentiation, with PKA playing a secondary role.

result: Presynaptic EPAC and PKCε are not required for postsynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses. A 1 Hz stimulation protocol induces LTP without PPF changes in both control and mice with presynaptic deletion of EPAC or PKCε.
evaluation: Claims C131-C145 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 5B-J) showing postsynaptic LTP is intact in mice with presynaptic EPAC or PKCε deletion. The unchanged PPF confirms the postsynaptic nature of this LTP form, and the intact LTP demonstrates specificity of EPAC-PKCε for presynaptic mechanisms.

result: Presynaptic EPAC and PKCε are not required for postsynaptic LTD at PF-PC synapses. The standard LTD induction protocol successfully induces LTD without PPF changes in both control and mice with presynaptic deletion of EPAC or PKCε.
evaluation: Claims C139-C144 are supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 6B-J) showing postsynaptic LTD is intact in mice with presynaptic EPAC or PKCε deletion. The unchanged PPF confirms the postsynaptic nature of this LTD form, further demonstrating the specificity of EPAC-PKCε for presynaptic plasticity.

result: Presynaptic deletion of EPAC or PKCε impairs basic motor performance when visual and vestibular systems are tested separately (OKR and VOR), but not when engaged simultaneously (VVOR). Both Rapgef3/4-dKO and Prkce-cKO mice show deficits in OKR and VOR gain and phase, but normal VVOR.
evaluation: Claims C146-C158 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 7B-G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C) showing consistent deficits in OKR and VOR but not VVOR across multiple mouse lines. The selective impairment pattern suggests EPAC-PKCε is important when sensory systems operate independently but can be compensated when they work together.

result: EPAC and PKCε are required for VOR phase reversal learning. Control mice show proper gain decrease and phase reversal during training, while Rapgef3/4-dKO, Rapgef3;Rapgef4-cKO, and Prkce-cKO mice show smaller gain reductions and prominent deficits in phase reversal learning, particularly on days 2-5.
evaluation: Claims C160-C165 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 7I-J, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) showing impaired VOR adaptation in EPAC and PKCε knockout mice. The temporal pattern (intact day 1, impaired days 2-5) suggests EPAC-PKCε is particularly important for consolidation or expression of learned motor adaptations.

result: The EPAC-PKCε signaling cascade regulates presynaptic LTP and motor learning through a novel mechanism involving threonine phosphorylation of RIM1α and assembly of the Rab3A-RIM1α-Munc13-1 complex. This pathway is critical for presynaptic LTP at PF-PC synapses and for cerebellar motor behavior, enriching the spectrum of cerebellar learning mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C166-C173 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are supported by the convergence of molecular (phosphorylation, protein interactions), structural (vesicle docking), electrophysiological (LTP, release), and behavioral (motor learning) data. The comprehensive multi-level evidence strongly supports the proposed signaling cascade and its functional importance.
